gao-gaoreports-gao-05-288r:
Information Resource Management Internal Control Issues, GAO-05-288R of March 10, 2005, is a side letter on shaky data in a farm housing study. GAO had used Agriculture data files to judge who got rural housing loans and grants from October 1998 through April 2004. The plan was to map 5 years of loans to towns with 2000 census data. Bad data cut the work to five states.

The letter tells what kinds of errors sat in the files. Names and places did not match the facts on the ground. It asks what checks the data shop runs to catch such flaws. Weak checks mean chiefs steer by false maps, GAO warns.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-338r:
Climate Change Assessment, GAO-05-338R of April 14, 2005, is a letter that faults a missed date for the nation's climate score card. A 1990 law tells the White House to sum up climate science at least each 4 years. The sum must weigh proof, list harms to land, health, and wealth, and chart trends 25 to 100 years out. A joint science plan took the task in 2002.

That plan set a path of 21 topic reports in July 2003. Congress asked GAO to test the path next to the law, on both time and scope. The date set by law had passed with no sum in hand, the title states.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-398r:
Human Capital, GAO-05-398R of April 21, 2005, is a letter that takes stock of a patchwork: each big agency now holds its own staff rule book. Congress gave NASA, Homeland Security, and Defense wide leave to shape pay, hire, and feat rules. The old one-size book is one size no more. A forum of pros met to ask if a shared frame should bind the set.

The forum found shared ground on ground rules, tests, and steps for any such frame. This letter adds the facts on what leave each named agency holds in law. It aims to feed the next talk on how wide reform should run.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-408r:
Department of Education's Update of the State and Other Tax Allowance, GAO-05-408R of March 22, 2005, is a letter on one small dial in the school aid math. Aid turns on what a home can pay. A tax dial cuts that sum by the state taxes a home bears. On December 23, 2004, the department reset the dial for award year 2005-2006. It used tax year 2002 data, by the same path a past plan took.

A January 21, 2005 GAO report had weighed that path and its flaws. Congress asked for a fresh view on the reset as made. The letter gives it, with the dial's reach on who gets aid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-468r:
Weak points in the arms export control system are set out in a GAO letter, GAO-05-468R, dated April 7, 2005. The State Department licenses arms exports and checks seller compliance with the law. It must keep U.S. arms from the wrong hands while letting lawful trade with allies proceed. The letter sums up GAO's February 2005 report on the system and a decade of related work.

The department had made no deep changes since the September 2001 attacks. Officials said none were needed, but that view rested on no systematic test of how well controls work. GAO pointed to fights over which items it controls. It also flagged weak checks on exports needing no prior approval. Enforcement teams faced tight budgets and thin staff. License handling times, after falling for years, began rising in fiscal year 2003. The letter warns that these flaws leave gaps in protection.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-498r:
Audit reports for the Air Force Sergeants Association are transmitted in GAO letter GAO-05-498R, dated June 10, 2005. The association serves current and retired Air Force enlisted members. Its work includes monthly magazines, yearly conventions, scholarships, and help on laws that affect members. The letter covers the fiscal years that ended April 30, 2004, and April 30, 2003.

Federal law requires chartered corporations to file yearly financial statements and to have them audited by an outside accountant. GAO read the statements, their notes, and the auditor's reports, and ran basic checks on the figures. It found no case where the reporting rules were broken. The auditors held that the statements were fairly presented under standard accounting rules. GAO did not run its own audit and gave no opinion of its own. The letter went to the chairman of the House Judiciary Committee.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-508r:
In GAO letter GAO-05-508R, dated June 10, 2005, the corporation under review is the Jewish War Veterans, U.S.A., National Memorial. It keeps a national memorial and museum in honor of Americans of the Jewish faith who served and fell in U.S. wars. The audit reports cover the fiscal years ended March 31, 2004, and March 31, 2003.

Under the charter law, the memorial must file yearly financial statements and have them audited by an outside accountant. GAO read those statements and the auditors' reports and applied analytical checks. It also held limited talks with the auditor about how reporting might be strengthened. The read turned up no instance of noncompliance with the law. The auditors' opinions held the statements fairly presented under U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. GAO gave no opinion of its own and did not audit the memorial.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-588r:
In GAO-05-588R (June 23, 2005), GAO reports on the fiscal year 2004 representation letter sent by the Department of Health and Human Services. The letter supports the audit of the whole government's financial statements. Each large agency must confirm its own figures in writing. GAO weighed this letter in five key areas and found room to improve in three of them.

The department left out its materiality thresholds, so readers cannot tell which matters it judged big enough to matter. Its letter carried 27 of the 29 standard representations that applied to it. The other 2 were present only in part. The summary of errors left uncorrected was also incomplete. It did not split errors in accounts with other agencies from errors in accounts with the public. GAO sent three recommendations to the acting chief financial officer. It asked the inspector general, working with the outside audit firm, to help fix future letters.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-598r:
Housing and Urban Development's fiscal year 2004 representation letter is examined in GAO-05-598R, a GAO letter dated July 22, 2005. Agency representation letters confirm the figures behind the government's audited financial statements. GAO checked this one in five key areas. Two areas needed improvement, and one of them involved the letter's core list of confirmations.

The letter included 24 of the 29 standard representations that applied to the department. Of the other 5, 3 were partial and 2 were not provided. The summary of uncorrected misstatements was also incomplete. It did not separate errors in accounts held with other agencies from errors in accounts held with the public. GAO made two recommendations to the acting deputy chief financial officer. The inspector general was asked to work with the department on later letters. In their replies, both offices said they will address the conditions GAO noted in the report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-608r:
Fiscal year 2004's letter from the Federal Communications Commission is assessed in GAO-05-608R (July 22, 2005). Of the five key areas GAO reviewed, one fell short. The letter stands behind the commission's own audited statements for that year. The commission included 24 of the 26 standard representations that applied to it. The other two were not provided at all.

GAO asked the Chief Financial Officer to include every applicable representation in future letters. It also asked the Inspector General, with the outside audit firm, to help the agency comply. The finance and inspector general offices replied that they would work to address the gap.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-638r:
Late comments from the defense department get their own airing in GAO-05-638R, a letter dated May 11, 2005. It follows an April 2005 report on troops' personal money troubles. The department's reply missed the printing deadline, so GAO prints it here with its own evaluation. The first study found deployed and home-based troops in like money shape, but deployment added pay snags. Almost 6,000 deployed troops got more than the set $250 monthly family allowance in January 2005 through confused procedures.

The department also lacks a way to judge its money-help programs. Services resisted outcome reporting, and the final rule dropped it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-668r:
A soybean fungus newly arrived in the United States is tracked in GAO letter GAO-05-668R (May 17, 2005). Asian soybean rust turned up in Louisiana in November 2004 and eight more southern states within weeks. It spreads to over 90 host plants and survived winter on kudzu in Florida. The farm department had planned since 2002, building a detection network and a strategy paper. That plan was still unfinished when the disease landed, and oversight money ran short.

In May 2005 the Secretary freed about $1.2 million in emergency funds for the season. The letter sums up work on sprays and resistant strains, with a state survey enclosed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-678r:
Federal pre-school programs still number 69, GAO letter GAO-05-678R reports on June 2, 2005. It updates a 2000 count made over fears of overlap. The search swept 254 candidate programs in the federal aid catalog. After applying three tests — direct aid, children under 5, a care or school setting — the same total emerged, now run by 10 agencies, one more than before. Sixteen programs left the list and 16 joined it.

The Education Department saw the most churn, dropping 11 and adding 5. Agencies disputed 13 entries; GAO kept all but 2 after review. The enclosed list names each program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-68r:
Money controls at the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights fail testing in GAO letter GAO-05-68R, sent March 7, 2005. Payroll held up: checks on $5.3 million found the sums substantially right. Travel and buying did not. In tests of $4.9 million of nonpayroll spending, records were so thin that GAO could not judge whether up to 18 percent of the sampled deals were valid at all.

The agency had no full written rulebook for handling money. Record keeping and rule enforcement were spotty across the board. The letter builds on years of GAO warnings about the commission's management.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-988r:
Follow-up answers on security clearances fill GAO-05-988R, a letter dated August 19, 2005. GAO had testified on June 28, 2005, at a hearing titled Access Delayed: Fixing the Security Clearance Process. A senator sent questions after that hearing. This letter answers them for the record.

The answers add detail on the Defense Department's clearance program. That program was the subject of the June testimony and of GAO's high-risk listing. Readers get the senator's concerns and GAO's replies side by side. The letter extends the public record on delays and fixes in clearance work. It pairs with the testimony it follows, giving Congress a fuller file for its oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-128r:
Health coverage for families of activated reservists is weighed in GAO-06-128R, a letter report from October 2005. When Guard and reserve members serve over 30 days, they fall under TRICARE, the military health system. Their spouses and dependents may choose TRICARE or keep private insurance. Past GAO work found that families who dropped private coverage hit snags in TRICARE. They struggled to find providers, prove eligibility, and grasp benefits. Some bills in Congress would pay a stipend so families can keep private coverage.

GAO compared the two paths on cost and care. The stipend approach is expected to cost more than TRICARE. It could, though, improve continuity of care for dependents. Keeping the same doctors matters most for family members with chronic conditions. The letter gives Congress a trade-off in plain terms. Paying more may buy smoother care for families during long activations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-158r: GAO-06-158R is a letter report dated October 7, 2005. It records GAO's review of audit reports for the National Woman's Relief Corps. The corps is the auxiliary to the Grand Army of the Republic. The reports cover fiscal years 2003 and 2002. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance. The auditor's opinion held that the corporation's financial statements were presented fairly on a modified cash basis of accounting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-198r:
Highway Trust Fund tax flows are checked in GAO-06-198R, a letter report dated November 4, 2005. GAO helped the Department of Transportation test one claim: that the net excise tax revenue sent to the Highway Trust Fund rests on sound records. The work covers the fiscal year that ended September 30, 2005. GAO ran a set of procedures agreed with the department. Such work tests set items rather than giving a full audit opinion.

The procedures examined the year's activity behind the sums sent to the fund. Excise taxes on fuel and other items feed the fund that pays for highways. GAO worked under government auditing standards, which include the attestation rules of the accounting profession. Those rules guide how such checks are run and reported. The letter gives the Transportation Department a verified base for the year's trust fund figures. It sits beside a twin letter on unemployment taxes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-278r:
A vast drug coverage switch for poor seniors is war-gamed in GAO-06-278R, a letter report dated December 16, 2005. The 2003 Medicare law created the Part D drug benefit. On January 1, 2006, about 6 million people on both Medicare and Medicaid were to move their drug cover to Part D. The Medicare agency mailed notices through 2005. It assigned each person to a drug plan and set auto-enrollment for those who did not choose. This letter reviews the backup plans for when the switch goes wrong.

Any gap in drug cover can harm people who need daily medicine. The letter checks what fallbacks exist if plans, pharmacies, or data fail at the switch. Backup planning is the theme: who acts, and how fast, when a beneficiary is turned away. The report captures the eve of one of the largest benefit moves in Medicare history.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-308r:
Two special powers granted to an economic development agency are checked in GAO-06-308R, a letter dated December 21, 2005. The 2004 law renewing the Economic Development Administration ordered regular review of both. One power lets savings from projects built under budget flow into new work. The other sets up performance awards for grantees that beat their targets. The letter reports how much spare money the agency had to send back to the Treasury.

Unused savings that return to the Treasury are chances lost for poor regions. An award system, done well, can push grantees to reach higher. Done poorly, it rewards paperwork over results. GAO sketches steps the agency could take to make the awards useful. The letter's scope is narrow by design. It watches two experiments in letting an agency keep and honor success. Future reviews will judge whether either power earned its keep.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-38r:
Four years of books for a group of noncommissioned officers get a clean review. Letter GAO-06-38R, dated October 7, 2005, covers the audit reports for the Non Commissioned Officers Association. The reports run for the years 2000 through 2003. The group helps veterans and their dependents and survivors. It also fosters social ties among its members and runs a service program for them.

By law, such chartered groups must present their assets, debts, income, and costs in yearly statements. An outside public accountant must audit those statements. GAO read the statements, the notes, and the reports of the auditor. It found no reportable case of failure to follow the law. The auditor said the statements were presented fairly under U.S. accounting rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-508r:
Mentoring pairs of adults and children sit behind this audit review. Letter GAO-06-508R, dated March 14, 2006, covers Big Brothers-Big Sisters of America. The audit report runs for the fiscal year ended March 31, 2003. The group's purpose is to make a positive difference in young lives. It does so mainly through one-to-one ties with caring adults. It helps children reach their highest potential.

Federal law requires chartered corporations to file yearly statements and obtain an independent audit. GAO read the statements and auditor's reports. It found no reportable instance of noncompliance. The auditors said the statements were presented fairly under U.S. accounting principles.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-688r:
Youth baseball books get a federal check in GAO-06-688R, a short GAO letter dated May 12, 2006. Little League Baseball holds a federal charter. It runs youth baseball and softball leagues in the United States and in other lands. The law says chartered groups must put out yearly financial statements. The statements must show what they own and owe, and what came in and went out. An outside public accountant must audit the statements each year, and GAO reviews the result.

For fiscal years 2003 and 2002, GAO reviewed the audit reports on the league's statements. GAO found no cases it had to report in which the league broke the law's rules for yearly statements. The outside auditor held that the statements were fairly shown in line with United States generally accepted accounting principles. GAO's letter sends that clean result to Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-768r:
Guidance for auditing benefit promises fills GAO-06-768R, a GAO letter dated June 29, 2006. GAO is the principal auditor of the consolidated financial statements of the United States government. Those statements carry huge estimates for federal employee and veteran benefit payables. The estimates rest on actuarial work, which projects future costs. GAO plans to use the work of inspectors general and hired accountants who audit agency statements.

The letter tells those auditors which methods to apply to the benefit estimates. GAO said a recent auditing standard on actuarial estimates fits this line item well. From fiscal year 2006, GAO planned to use that standard as its guide. The joint federal Financial Audit Manual supplies the shared framework. The guidance aims for one consistent approach across many audit teams.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-778r:
Written answers to Congress on air traffic research fill GAO-06-778R, a letter report dated May 17, 2006. A House panel had held a hearing on March 29, 2006, titled The Future of Air Traffic Control: The R&D Agenda. Members later sent GAO questions for the record. A request dated April 26, 2006, asked GAO to answer them. The questions concerned research paths for the next generation air traffic system.

GAO based its responses on its past and ongoing work on air traffic control. GAO did not seek agency comments, since the answers drew on products that had already faced comment. The responses were prepared in May 2006 under government auditing standards. Readers get GAO's considered views on research priorities, in question-and-answer form. The letter is a supplement to the hearing record, not a fresh audit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-78r:
A stopgap drug card program for seniors is reviewed in GAO-06-78R, a letter report dated October 31, 2005. The Medicare law of 2003 added a full drug benefit starting January 1, 2006. Until then, a temporary discount card program was meant to ease drug costs. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services had to build the card program in about six months. GAO judged how the agency solicited, judged, and approved card sponsors, and how it oversaw them.

GAO found that the agency's processes were shaped by that six-month rush. It used a noncompetitive solicitation in which all qualified applicants could take part. Application design and review were likewise built for speed. GAO's letter shows the trade-offs of launching a national program on a deadline. It also records lessons for the full benefit that followed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-838r:
Defense contracting abuse is the warning in GAO-06-838R, a letter report GAO issued on July 7, 2006. The Defense Department awards huge and growing sums to contractors each year. That scale leaves it open to fraud, waste, and abuse. Recent years produced many cases in which taxpayer dollars were misused or wasted. GAO summed up the department's exposure and its response so far.

GAO concluded that the department will stay vulnerable while contract awards remain so large. Cases will keep surfacing where controls fail. The department had begun to respond as cases came to light. New policies and tighter practices were in motion. But GAO cautioned that the impact of those fixes would show only over time. The letter is a standing alert on the risks of heavy reliance on contractors.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-848r:
Pay sent to soldiers who never reported for duty is exposed in GAO-06-848R, a letter report dated July 28, 2006. GAO had reported for years on pay errors hitting Army Guard and Reserve soldiers. A labor-heavy, error-prone pay process caused many of them. So did weak staffing and pay systems that did not talk to personnel systems. This letter covers a sharper case: mobilized soldiers who were in deserter status yet kept being paid.

GAO concluded that the Army stays open to this abuse unless it targets the unique risks of desertion cases. Soldiers who fail to report when their units mobilize do not meet their service duty. Flawed systems and slow status updates let some accept pay they did not earn. GAO urged the Army to identify and blunt those risks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-858r:
A dormant satellite television loan program is closed out in GAO-06-858R, a letter report dated July 7, 2006. The LOCAL Television Act aimed to bring local TV signals to underserved areas through federal loan guarantees. The act's Section 1006 requires GAO to report each year on the program's spending. GAO has done so since fiscal year 2002. This letter gives the status for fiscal year 2005.

GAO reported that no loan guarantees had ever been approved under the program. No budget resources were on hand, or expected, for future guarantees. On December 13, 2004, the program's board authorized closing out one of its two contracts. The other contract had expired. The letter is a brief annual record of a program that never truly launched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-928r:
Stryker vehicle upkeep, and a planned shift in who does it, is examined in GAO letter GAO-06-928R, dated September 5, 2006. Stryker brigades were built for fast deployment, with lean stocks of parts and staff. Contract crews held the largest support role, fixing the vehicles and running their supply chain.

On November 1, 2005 the Army set changes to that support. One change would swap contract fixers for soldiers, now that the Army can train its own. GAO weighed the shift and its risks. The letter urges the Army to name clear plans for the snags the change will bring, before they bite in the field.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1048r:
Monthly data on attacks in Iraq should reach the public on time, GAO argues in letter GAO-07-1048R, dated September 28, 2007. Enemy-launched attacks are a key gauge of Iraq's security. In spring 2007 about 30,000 added U.S. troops went to Iraq. The total hit about 160,000 by mid-June 2007.

Since 2004 GAO has shared attack trends with Congress, in secret and open forms. Defense bodies helped it clear the data each month for open use. The letter gives data through August 31, 2007. It urges the Defense Department to give Congress and the public the monthly figures in a timely way itself.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1088r:
Missile warning satellites, over cost and late, are weighed with their backup plan in GAO letter GAO-07-1088R, dated September 12, 2007. The Space Based Infrared System began in 1996, to replace the old launch warning net. It was set to fly by 2004, at about $4.2 billion.

After 11 years of tech strain and restarts, the price tops $10.4 billion. The first launch is set for 2008. In 2006 the Defense Department began a rival system as a hedge. GAO judged if the main program can meet its new cost, time, and skill aims for its first two craft. It also judged the call to build the rival.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1138r:
Personnel counts at the Air National Guard are firmer, but not yet sound, GAO states in letter GAO-07-1138R, dated July 31, 2007. In September 2004 the Guard found flaws in its strength data for new recruits. Two pay groups, for recruits in training and those awaiting it, were mixed up. Their pay rates differ a lot, so budget sums swung.

In May 2007 GAO told Congress the Guard had taken fair steps to fix the data. Flaws stayed in a key check tool, and in the stand-in data used in the mean time. The letter names added steps the Guard should take, so the strength figures Congress sees can be trusted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1148r:
A defense report on predatory lending to troops is checked in GAO letter GAO-07-1148R, dated August 31, 2007. Bad debts can hurt unit morale, clearances, and careers. A 2006 law told the Defense Department to report on loans that prey on troops and their families, and on its plans to teach and shield them.

Industry groups then faulted that report's build and advice. Congress asked GAO to review it. GAO judged the department's approach and support for its claims. The report did cover the points law required, GAO found. But backing is thin for some findings and some advice. The letter shows how proof standards apply even to a report on harm.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-148r:
No one knows how many Americans face domestic violence or stalking each year. GAO explained why in GAO-07-148R, a letter dated November 13, 2006. A 2006 law ordered GAO to study the data on these crimes. The crimes covered are domestic violence, sexual assault, dating violence, and stalking. Victims include men, women, youth, and children. This letter covers the first of two study questions.

National surveys and crime systems each cover only part of the picture, GAO found. They use different definitions of the crimes. Their scopes cover different groups of people. Because of that, their figures cannot be merged into one national rate. The gap limits sound choices on grants and programs for victims. The Justice and Health departments had early joint work toward uniform data. GAO gave them four steps to close the gaps. Those steps include using common definitions in federal research.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-168r:
A 1998 law let many Haitian nationals already in the United States become permanent residents. GAO's fifteenth report under that law is GAO-07-168R, dated November 9, 2006. The Haitian Refugee Immigration Fairness Act requires a report every 6 months. Each report counts applications filed and approved, by category. Categories cover asylum applicants, parolees, and children without parents. Dependents such as spouses and children are counted too.

Through September 30, 2006, the immigration services agency had received 40,298 applications. It had approved 16,616 of them. The immigration review office had 1,947 applications filed with it. It had approved 755 of those. The letter gives the full breakdown of filings and approvals by category. Reports in this series will continue until every application has been finally decided. The counts let Congress track how fast the special program is moving.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-228r:
For the first time, higher-income seniors will pay more for Medicare Part B coverage. GAO reviewed the rollout in GAO-07-228R, a letter dated November 17, 2006. The new income-based premiums start January 1, 2007. About 1.65 million beneficiaries will pay more. The trigger is income over $80,000 for singles and $160,000 for couples. Premiums can rise to 80 percent of full program cost over 3 years. The Social Security Administration must set and collect the new amounts.

The agency had a tight window to do the math, GAO found. It had about a month to set each premium. Notices were set to go out in late November 2006. Beneficiaries then had 60 days to appeal. They could also seek a fresh review after a major income drop. GAO warned of a surge in field office visits. Short time frames and heavy workloads could slow the launch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-298r:
Knowing what programs truly cost helps managers choose well, but one department's cost data is scattered. GAO surveyed the Interior Department in GAO-07-298R, dated May 24, 2007. The review is part of a series covering 10 large civilian agencies. Cost accounting rules come from a 1990 law and federal standards. GAO asked how the department builds cost figures. It also asked how managers use them.

No single system produces the department's cost data, GAO found. Bureaus pull figures from separate financial and workload systems. Checks on nonfinancial data are thin. Bureaus split shared costs by unlike methods. One bureau counts facilities while the department counts floor space. The department is building one integrated system with a cost module. Managers do use cost data for budgets, fees, and work reviews. The department agreed with six of GAO's eight recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-318r:
The whistleblower agency's own case counts have wobbled because of its tracking software. GAO audited the system in GAO-07-318R, a letter dated February 16, 2007. The Office of Special Counsel reports its caseload to Congress yearly. Two earlier GAO reviews found mismatched case totals. GAO tested 158 case files against the database. It asked whether the agency had fixed the gaps.

Core data proved reliable enough for reporting, GAO found. Dates and case types matched source files. Small summary gaps remain, within the agency's stated 3 percent tolerance. Mixed query methods cause most of the drift. The deeper flaw is process, GAO said. The system was built without a structured life cycle method. Requirements, tests, and changes went undocumented. That leaves untested data fields in doubt. The agency head accepted the documentation advice. He disputed the life cycle finding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-328r: A three-year span of audits is the subject of GAO-07-328R, dated January 26, 2007. The letter reviews audit reports for the American Council of Learned Societies. They cover fiscal years ended September 30 in 2005, 2004, and 2003. Each report found the statements presented fairly under U.S. accounting principles. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance across the three years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-568r: The VA's job-rehab contracting was improving in 2007 — GAO's letter says managing the service deals had gotten better, with real challenges left. The findings credit the gains while listing the gaps. The letter's theme: wounded veterans deserve well-run help, not well-meant chaos.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-668r: Jewish war veterans' books got the audit in 2007 — GAO's letter reviews the organization's financial statements for the year. The findings give the formal opinion for the record. The letter shows every chartered cause, however honored, faces the same ledger check.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-688r: Fuel-price swings were whipsawing the Pentagon's budget in 2007 — GAO's letter reviews how the department planned for the volatility. The findings test the hedging math in detail. The letter's question: was the war machine really budgeting for the pump price?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-768r: Stretching federal housing dollars was the theme in 2007 — GAO's letter explores leveraging public money for homes, blocks, and jobs. The findings showcase the multiplier game in action. The letter's pitch: make each federal dollar recruit private ones to the cause.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-878r: The home-loan banks' new stock rule was too fresh to judge in 2007 — GAO's letter says the impact on affordable housing could not yet be told. The findings counsel patience with the verdict. The letter's caution: do not grade the harvest before the planting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-908r: New Orleans' pumps got a procurement probe in 2007 — GAO's letter examines the Corps' buying of drainage-canal pumping systems. The findings test the post-Katrina deals. The letter's stakes: the pumps that keep a city dry must be bought right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-918r: The next-gen air system faced its grilling in 2007 — GAO's letter answers the hearing's leftover questions on the JPDO blueprint. The responses supply the missing detail on costs and timing. The findings feed the long debate over rebuilding the nation's skies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-928r: Air-traffic modernization got its Q&A in 2007 — GAO's letter answers Congress's follow-ups from the hearing on the control system's future. The responses fill the gaps the testimony left open. The findings keep the modernization debate supplied with facts instead of slogans.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1038r: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at various Issues Led to the Termination of the United States-Canada Shared Border Management Pilot Project. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-148r: GAO wrote Congress in 2007 with an honest shrug: nobody could say if the 2005 bankruptcy rewrite hurt child support. The data to run a real study just did not exist. The letter is a rare official admission of a blind spot — Congress changed the rules for broke parents, then built no way to see how kids fared.
